Science.title: Massive carbon stocks in grasslands are ignored by climate finance
Science.summary: Open ecosystems—nonforested landscapes such as grasslands, shrublands and savannas—can store vast amounts of carbon while supporting water supply, biodiversity and other ecosystem services. Yet the potential of open ecosystems to serve as natural climate solutions remains ignored by policies that privilege forests. So reports a team of researchers in a policy brief published today in PLANTS, PEOPLE, PLANET.

Science.title: As flood risk rises, some communities question the idea of resilience
Science.summary: Climate change is increasing flood risk across the U.K. As floods become more frequent and intense, communities are increasingly encouraged to become resilient and "live with water." Science.title: Chaos makes sense of market movements in a crisis

Science.title: Scientists uncover the molecular pillars that shape our cells' powerpacks
Science.summary: Mitochondria are the tiny powerpacks that supply most of the energy our cells need. Their ability to generate this energy relies on a distinctive architecture: two membranes, one tucked inside the other, separated by a narrow gap called the intermembrane space (IMS). This tiny space helps sustain the chemistry of energy production, making its organization critical to how these cellular powerpacks function.

Science.title: Study maps the human side of flood risk
Science.summary: When heavy rain hits a city, knowing where water will accumulate is only part of the picture. Who lives in the affected buildings? How might flooding disrupt their lives? And where could additional support make the greatest difference?

Science.title: Mechanism behind PARP1-mediated DNA repair characterized, offering insight into targeted cancer therapy
Science.summary: When DNA is damaged, cellular processes respond and repair the DNA. Inhibiting DNA damage repair can be therapeutically beneficial in cancers with genetic vulnerabilities related to DNA damage response. Scientists at St. Jude Children's Research Hospital have uncovered a mechanism behind how this process works, which may have implications for cancer treatment. The results were published today in Molecular Cell.

Science.title: An ancient virus in chimpanzee DNA switches off a gene that is active in humans
Science.summary: Humans and chimpanzees share almost all their genes. Despite this, our brains have developed in different ways. Researchers at Lund University in Sweden have now shown that a viral pandemic dating back several million years is likely to be part of the explanation.

Science.title: Paleolithic human DNA reveals east-west connections across Ice Age Europe
Science.summary: More than 30,000 years ago, people associated with one of Europe's major Paleolithic cultures (the Gravettian) were more interconnected than previously thought. An international research team led by the University of Vienna has uncovered new genetic evidence of long-distance connections between these populations. Published in Science Advances, the study combines genomic data from rare human remains with human DNA preserved in cave sediments.

Science.title: Breakthrough PTSD treatment achieves 68% remission rate in clinical trial
Science.summary: A newly FDA-cleared PTSD treatment uses personalized brain mapping and magnetic stimulation to target abnormal brain activity, with a clinical trial reporting a 52% reduction in symptoms and 68% remission. Science.title: Scientists demonstrate AI-designed enzyme for drug synthesis

Science.summary: How can the identity of pluripotent stem cells be determined more reliably during their differentiation? Science.summary: The Orion Nebula is a large star-forming region visible to the naked eye. Some of the young stars in the nebula are surrounded by disks of gas and dust in which planets form. Radiation from the massive central star, 1 Ori C1 (Theta-1 Orionis C1), gradually strips material from these disks, giving them shapes that resemble tadpoles.

Science.title: Scientists discover a surprising double benefit of exercise for Parkinson’s
Science.summary: A seven-year study found that people with Parkinson’s disease who were more physically active experienced slower declines in memory, thinking, and movement abilities. Those exercising more than eight hours per week showed almost no average cognitive decline, suggesting that staying active may offer important benefits as the disease progresses.

Science.title: From sea anemone to human fertility: A new research organism for understanding meiosis
Science.summary: Every egg cell and sperm cell depends on meiosis, a tightly choreographed process in which chromosomes find their partners, exchange genetic material and then divide. When meiosis goes awry in humans, the consequences can include infertility, miscarriage and birth defects.

Science.title: Rare fossils reveal what ancient Denisovans may have looked like
Science.summary: Whenever anything is written about the Denisovans, the word "mysterious" is almost guaranteed to appear. Science.title: Plain silicon grating reveals a hidden 'twist' in light from electron beams
Science.summary: In 1953, two physicists showed that an electron beam skimming past a grating emits light whose color depends only on the electron's speed and the grating's spacing. Known as Smith-Purcell radiation, this phenomenon has become a useful tool for building compact, tunable light sources and tracking particle beams without touching them.

Science.title: El Niño Then and Now

Science.summary: Researchers at the MRC Laboratory of Medical Sciences (LMS) have developed a new way to make glowing biological reporters more accurate, allowing scientists to track gene activity in living plants over days, weeks and potentially even months and years. The approach could help researchers study how plants respond to disease, pests and environmental stress, while opening the door to similar applications in animal and human disease models.

Science.title: One of Earth’s most powerful supervolcanoes is refilling with fresh magma
Science.summary: Deep beneath Japan’s Kikai caldera, a massive magma reservoir is refilling 7,300 years after one of the most powerful volcanic eruptions in Earth's recent geological history. Scientists used underwater seismic surveys to reveal a vast store of magma that appears to have accumulated since the ancient catastrophe. The discovery could help explain how supervolcanoes like Yellowstone and Toba rebuild their magma supplies.

Science.title: Counting magnetic flux quanta offers new way to measure photon numbers

Science.title: Bacteria reinvent their weapons through selection, chance and gene swapping
Science.summary: Many of the most potent antibiotics originate from bacteria. A large proportion belong to a class of compounds known as nonribosomal peptides (NRP). They are produced by large bacterial enzyme machineries—the nonribosomal peptide synthetases, or NRPS for short. These function like molecular assembly lines: Similar to the stations in a car factory, where new parts are added to the car at each step, several specialized modules string together amino acid by amino acid to build a peptide.

Science.title: Scientists find key to predicting some El Niño events 12 months ahead

Science.title: Potatoes could be the secret to better plant-based meat, say food scientists

Science.title: 'Stupendously large black holes' aren't a major component of dark matter, study finds

Science.title: Scientists discover a hidden messaging system deep inside the brain
Science.summary: A tiny region deep within the brain has surprised scientists by revealing a remarkably sophisticated communication system. Previously thought to broadcast the same chemical signal throughout the brain, this region actually sends targeted messages that help control learning, attention, and behavior, according to new research in mice.

Science.title: Never finishing the fight: Where did Xbox go wrong with Halo?
Science.summary: After a failed soft reboot and a remake of the original, the Halo universe is facing yet another major creative shift. But has Xbox learned any lessons this time?

Science.title: Can we stop antibiotic resistance from ruining promising drugs before they reach patients?
Science.summary: What if we could predict early in drug development which antibiotics bacteria are most likely to become resistant to? In a review published in Nature Reviews Microbiology, researchers from the HUN-REN Biological Research Centre, Szeged (HUN-REN BRC Szeged) and the Hungarian Centre of Excellence for Molecular Medicine (HCEMM) in Szeged propose a five-step decision-making framework that could help identify resistance risks early, refine promising drug candidates and prevent costly failures.

Science.title: Christina Applegate misdiagnosis: Why can MS be difficult to diagnose?
